lucrative

LOO-kruh-tiv — starts like 'loot'; a lucrative deal brings in plenty of loot. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Lucrative is producing a great deal of profit.

The small startup signed an unexpectedly lucrative contract that tripled its yearly revenue overnight.

Example

A teenager starts mowing lawns for five dollars each over the summer. Within two years, word spreads, he hires three friends to help, buys better equipment, and now runs a small but lucrative business that earns him more in a summer than most part-time jobs pay in a year.

Growing into something that earns real, substantial profit is exactly what makes a business lucrative. Unlike 'busy,' which just means a lot of activity, lucrative specifically means highly profitable.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rewarding: Rewarding means the payoff satisfies you — and the reward can be pride, gratitude, or money. Lucrative is strictly about money, and a lot of it: a volunteer job can be deeply rewarding while paying nothing, but nothing unprofitable is ever lucrative.

moneymaking: Moneymaking is the plain, neutral label for anything that brings money in, however modestly — a moneymaking hobby might clear a few dollars a week. Lucrative claims far more: the profit is unusually large or impressive, not merely present.

gainful: Gainful describes work that earns an income — gainful employment simply means a paying job, with nothing said about how much. Lucrative raises the bar: not just paid, but unusually well paid, producing profit on an impressive scale.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ruinous: causing serious financial loss

worthless: having no financial or practical value

Where it sits · how strongly the money pours in

profitable → lucrative → booming

profitable vs. lucrative: Profitable is a milder, more general word than lucrative — something profitable simply earns money, while lucrative implies the profit is especially large or impressive.

booming vs. lucrative: Booming can feel even bigger than lucrative: lucrative describes strong, steady profit, but booming suggests rapid, explosive growth on top of that profit.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — lucr-: profit, gain (Latin (lucrum))

suffix — -ative: tending to, having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Latin lucrum meant 'profit, gain.' Something lucrative, at its root, has a strong tendency to produce exactly that — real financial gain.

Use the root in a new word: lucre: The preacher's sermon that morning kept circling back to lucre.
